body: So we’ve curated 143 presents to reclaim holiday shopping as a joyous activity. We recruited seasoned writers and shopping experts to get into the holiday spirit early, vetting gifts across categories such as kitchen, home, tech and more. For months, we cooked, ate, traveled, hiked, ran, showered and slept with test products by our side. And we roped in our mothers, cats, dogs and the kids in our lives to make sure these gifts really work for the people (and pets!) they are meant for.

Our comprehensive list spans safe bets (who doesn’t like chocolate?) to niche recommendations ( butter-shaped candle, anyone?). You’ll find a range of prices from a $6 cleaning cloth for a notoriously dirty laptop owner to a sophisticated trenchcoat for your stylish sister. Happy gifting.
Don’t see anything that catches your eye? Email us at thefilterus@theguardian.com for help finding a gift for your trickiest recipient.

articles.title: ‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
articles.summary: The world has become accustomed to concerns about the male loneliness epidemic. But research suggests women are just as lonely. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads. No one would think of Sasha* as lonely, least of all Sasha herself.
body: “All those things that you read about, about why men might be lonely – they don’t maintain one-on-one friendships, or they’re not good at reaching out, or their conversations aren’t deep and meaningful – none of those issues apply to me,” she says. “I’m a very socially connected person.”

Yet Sasha often felt lonely during her first year of motherhood, even when she was surrounded by other people. (All case studies’ names have been changed.) She attributes it now to the intensity of the experience. “It’s the identity shift of your first child, having no idea of what you’re doing, learning on the fly … You feel alone.”

We’re living through a global crisis of loneliness, with the World Health Organization (WHO) declaring it a priority for public health, but it’s hard to miss that the coverage and conversation has been overwhelmingly focused on men.
Global Google searches for “male loneliness” spiked suddenly in mid-2023, and have since seen frequent surges; interest in “female loneliness”, meanwhile, has remained a trickle.

But research suggests women are just as lonely.

articles.title: ‘Don’t lie to me to get free stuff’: how small businesses are fighting back against influencers
articles.summary: From diva-like behaviour to freebie requests that never result in a review, ‘entitled’ content creators are a growing blight on small-business owners. Now entrepreneurs are calling them out. Nicole Flanagin remembers exactly the moment an influencer came after her business.
body: The 41-year-old was already having a bad 24 hours. A mother of four, Flanagin also works at a pet rescue shelter and had spent the previous day unsuccessfully fighting for a dog not to be put down. She got home exhausted and promptly conked out in bed. Then she woke up to the message.

The video began innocuously enough with a local influencer sitting in her parked car. “For those of you who know me,” she stated, “I do reviews of local businesses. One very special thing about me is I don’t make bad reviews – but I’m kinda mad right now!” The woman had just taken her child to an unnamed cafe with “animals you can pet”, only to be coldly turned away because she had got its visiting hours wrong. In the influencer’s telling, she began bargaining with staff to try to let the girl into the area where the animals were kept. No dice. Her daughter started “literally bawling her eyes out … and they were just, like, standing there staring”.

articles.title: ‘None of them had ever seen an eclipse in real life’: Maurice Bakley’s best phone picture
articles.summary: An ​e​lementary school ​w​atch party turned into a great opportunity to take a child’s-eye view of a spectacular astral phenomenon. Maurice Bakley was chaperoning an eclipse watch party at his son’s elementary school in Arlington, Virginia, when he took this photograph.
body: “The boys in the photo, one of whom is my son, are part of a tight group of friends. They’ve known each other since kindergarten through their bilingual Spanish immersion school,” Bakley says. “They were eight and nine years old at the time, and none of them had ever seen an eclipse in real life.”

As the kids were sitting cross-legged on the ground, Bakley made sure to get down to their level for this shot. “A top-down angle wouldn’t have conveyed the same intimacy,” he says. “I approach mobile photography in the same way that I used to approach SLR photography, which includes being intentional in both the capture and the edit.”

When editing, Bakley applied a film-like colour grading, and a touch of blur to the background to focus attention on the boys. He also opted for a square crop. “I don’t crop in that way often,” he says, “but it suited this composition, lending a more timeless, nostalgic feeling.”

articles.title: What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out
articles.summary: Writer Bridget Knowles seeks out the Austrian philosophy behind Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort in Austria’s Großarl Valley that encourages guests to get in the buff.
body: When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großar l Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened.

In Austria, being naked isn’t just a physical state. It’s an emotional state, too. Austrians strip themselves down, both figuratively and literally, to achieve a mindset they call “Lebensgefühl,” a deep mind-body awareness and lifestyle that is difficult to define, let alone translate.
Großar l Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria.

Originally a German concept, the idea stems from “Lebensphilosophie,” a 19th-century intellectual movement popularized by big name thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche, Georg Simmel, and Wilhelm Dilthey. Translating to “philosophy of life,” the framework is centered around the idea that life can only be understood from within oneself, as opposed to through applying external dogmas like logic and science. Life, according to this framework, is a joyful, vibrant, and embodied experience—a philosophy now widely integrated and cherished by Germany ’s neighbor, Austria.

articles.title: A TikToker Went Viral for Kayaking 500 Miles of Congolese River—and Started an Even Bigger Conversation
articles.summary: ‘Extreme athlete’ Ash Dykes and his Congolese guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire on the story they had hoped to tell through their arduous adventure.
body: In October, adventurer Ash Dykes, local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire, and cameraman Will Perez embarked on a 500-mile kayaking trip in Republic of the Congo.

When Dykes posted the minute-and-a-half-long video of this “encounter” in the Sangha—cause still unknown—the post racked up over 8 million views on TikTok. The thousands-deep comments section, full of viewers hooked as to what might happen next, burst with theories: Some swore that Mami Wata, a water spirit said to frequent the riverbanks, had caused the sudden movement. One user mused that the three men were in “a real game of Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while others zoomed in on Perez’s visibly tense expression. Another user quipped: “I quit my job to focus on this expedition.”
The Congo Basin is the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike.
points: ‘Extreme athlete’ Ash Dykes and his Congolese guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire on the story they had hoped to tell through their arduous adventure.

articles.title: Stop Using Your Phone for Touch-Ups—This Travel Makeup Mirror Is Foldable and Lightweight
articles.summary: About the size of a Kindle, my favorite travel makeup mirror is slim enough to fit in any tote or backpack.
body: The pre-flight touch-up was not the only time Deanna's travel makeup mirror came in handy on our trip. One night before dinner, as 12 girls simultaneously got ready, she and I realized we were running short on bathroom mirrors. Rather than wait for the bathroom to clear and be forced to rush, or be late, we took turns doing our makeup with her travel mirror. Before we landed back at Newark Airport after the trip, I had already ordered Funtouch's travel makeup mirror for myself on Amazon.

After a few months of having my own, I can honestly say this $17 travel accessory is worth every penny. While I initially envisioned using it on the plane or a crowded girls trip, it's proven handy on numerous occasions. Most recently, on a trip to Newport, Rhode Island, I pulled out my foldable travel mirror and did my makeup en-route. It was a relief to arrive at The Vanderbilt hotel looking and feeling put together, without having to sit through the whole four-hour car ride with a full face of makeup on first thing in the morning.
